title: The Lady and the Duke
full_review:
Director Eric Rohmer weaves a visually interesting tale of French history, but one which requires unwavering attention without providing much in return in the stuffy drama "The Lady & The Duke" (Sony Pictures Classics).

Inspired by the memoirs of the titular lady, Grace Elliott (played by Lucy Russell), the film spins a lush saga about keeping one's honor during a period of political terror. Grace, a displaced aristocratic Englishwoman, has taken to her new country with fervor. Despite the increasing danger, she remains steadfastly loyal to King Louis XVI during the French Revolution and the ensuing Reign of Terror.

Rohmer has drawn from the passages in the memoirs that describe Grace's relationship with her former lover, Phillippe, Duke of Orlean (Jean-Claude Dreyfus), and five crucial incidents during the French Revolution. The Duke urges her to flee, but having embraced Gallic life, she refuses. It is not that she is blinded to the real danger, but simply faithful to her Royalist opinions and loyal to the bonds of friendship she has formed in France, especially to the duke.

The film is spurred on by two key scenes. In the first, the Lady Grace manages to convince the duke to rescue an outlaw and personal enemy. This situation builds a considerable amount of suspense and tension as the outlaw is hidden between Grace's mattress and bedspring, while she uses reverse psychology to discourage the army general from searching her bed. And employing guile and affection, she manages to persuade the duke to ensure the man's safety.

In the second, she fails to keep the duke, a cousin of the king but nonetheless a supporter of revolutionary ideas, from voting for the king's execution. This rift in their friendship in unavoidable, but their affection for each other somehow surmounts their political differences.

Although there are a few gruesome images, such as of a woman's head at the end of a stake, the film's main thrust is eloquent conversation between men and women of a certain distinction. But this requires the audience's full concentration, which becomes tiresome as the film drags on past the two hour mark.

Visually, the film is arresting, sweetly naive and even peculiar. Rohmer commissioned painter Jean-Baptiste Marot to create 37 canvasses, based on paintings, illustrations and maps of the day. The actors were filmed against a blue screen, then digitally incorporated with proper scale and perspective, giving the film a 3-D effect. While in the outdoor scenes the actors seem to be strolling through painted sketches, in the indoor scenes, the thespians are shot in tight chamber-drama style, as if it were a filmed stage production. This visual style is somewhat ingenious, but instead of enhancing the main story, it detracts because it is so jarringly different from the usual.

"The Lady & The Duke" is an acquired taste that moviegoers may find a bit overwhelming.

Due to a few grisly images, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
